executive_summary: EUR/USD closed at 1.11674 on 2026-10-30, against an ECB reference rate of 1.1172 the same day, after touching about 1.11 on 29 October, the weakest level since May 2025; the euro lost 0.67% over one month, 3.17% over three months, 4.75% over six months and 3.62% over a year, and it fell against all ten G10+SGD peers in October [6][7]. The narrative is an energy-driven stagflation shock layered on French fiscal stress: Dutch TTF gas traded at EUR100/MWh on 28 October for the first time since December 2022 with EU storage near 75% full, euro-area HICP rose to 3.8% in September with core at 2.5%, and the OAT-Bund spread reached a 15-year high on 22-23 October [8][14][37]. The ECB held the deposit rate at 2.50% on 29 October after hikes in June and September, unanimously but after debating a hike, and Lagarde announced she will step down after the February 2027 meeting; markets price more than an 80% chance of a December hike and about 75bp of further tightening in total [1][2][5][6]. That leaves the deposit rate 137.5bp below the Fed midpoint of 3.875%, where a 10-2 vote with two hike dissents keeps a December Fed move live at about 77% on a futures-derived calculation [7][33]. Valuation pulls the other way: World Bank PPP factors put fair EUR/USD near 1.41, a 20.7% undervaluation, although the BIS real effective rate at 103.27 sits at the 67th percentile of its last 33 months and so is not cheap on a trade-weighted basis [20][21]. The tension is positioning: CFTC legacy speculators were net short 143,900 contracts in the week to 27 October, beyond the 100,000-contract level that has marked past EUR extremes, and leveraged funds hold their largest short of the 26 weeks since May at 71,574 contracts [39]. We are Bearish tactically (weighted score -0.30, conviction 3, overall confidence 54%) with a 4-week base case of 1.1050, and Bearish strategically (-0.41, conviction 3, confidence 55%) with a 6-month base case of 1.0900, 353 pips below the 6-month futures-implied forward of 1.1253, because the terms-of-trade shock, the French budget calendar and an ECB path that we think is over-priced by about 25bp dominate an undervaluation that needs a catalyst to matter.

tactical.analysis: The ECB deposit facility rate of 2.50% (MRO 2.65%, marginal lending 2.90%) was left unchanged on 29 October after 25bp hikes in June and September, and it ranks joint sixth of the ten G10+SGD rate-setters with Canada [1][3]. It sits 137.5bp below the Fed midpoint of 3.875%, 125bp below the BoE, 200bp below Norges Bank and 210bp below the RBA, and above only the Riksbank (+75bp), the BoJ (+125bp) and the SNB (+250bp) [33]. The two-year Schatz at 3.02% on 30 October is 52bp above the deposit rate, consistent with roughly two further hikes; over October it fell between 4bp (Trading Economics) and 18bp (a second daily series, which reads 3.06%), while the 10-year Bund fell 21-24bp to 3.32% (3.40% on the second series), so both levels are best available, flagged, as of 2026-10-30 [25][26]. Against the US two-year at 4.67% on 28 October the front-end gap is about 165bp in the dollar's favour, and the 10-year gap is 161bp (Treasury 4.934%) [7][27]. Markets put more than an 80% probability on a 17 December hike and about 75bp of further ECB tightening in total, which on our own sum of the 2.50% deposit rate and about 75bp implies a terminal near 3.25% [5][6]. Our own assessment is a 70% probability of a December hike to 2.75% and a terminal rate of 3.00% by March 2027, so we see the curve over-pricing the ECB by about 25bp, with the risk concentrated in 2027 after Lagarde's departure. The Fed side is also live: after a 10-2 hold with Cook and Hammack voting to hike, a 9 December move to 4.00-4.25% had a probability of about 77% on 30 October on a futures-derived calculation, so the expected change in the policy differential over the next six weeks is close to zero [7][33]. The CME futures roll for EUR/USD, observed 2026-10-28, is 151.8bp annualised against a 137.5bp policy gap; the 14bp excess captures expected Fed-over-ECB tightening plus the cross-currency basis and confirms that the market sees no narrowing of the dollar's carry advantage [40]. Tactically that is Bearish for the euro: the carry gap is wide and stable, and the asymmetric risk around 17 December is a dovish disappointment rather than a hawkish surprise.

tactical.what_is_priced: The curve prices a December ECB hike as near-certain and, on our sum of the deposit rate and about 75bp priced, a terminal near 3.25%; we put December at 70% and the terminal at 3.00%. Because a futures-derived calculation puts the Fed's own December hike at about 77%, the ECB is the side with more room to disappoint, and a 25bp repricing of the 2027 strip would cost EUR/USD about 50-80 pips on the front-end sensitivity of the last two months.

strategic.analysis: Over six months both central banks are tightening, so the question is whether the 137.5bp differential narrows; our base case is that it does not [1][33]. The ECB's September projections put HICP at 3.0% for 2026, 2.5% for 2027 and 2.1% for 2028, with core at 2.5%, 2.6% and 2.3%; inflation returning near 2% by 2028 caps how far the Governing Council needs to go [4]. UBS Global Research expects 2.75% in December and a 'presumably final' 3.00% in March 2027, while its wealth arm calls December the last hike and describes that as more dovish than markets, which price about 75bp more [5]. We side with a 3.00% terminal, which is 25bp below the market and implies a 2.75-3.00% deposit rate across the strategic horizon. The Fed, with core PCE at 3.1% in September and two dissents for a hike, is more likely than not to reach 4.00-4.25% by March 2027, keeping the midpoint gap at 125-137.5bp [33][34]. The Bund curve at +30bp on 2s10s is flat for a hiking cycle, which tells us the market already doubts the ECB's ability to tighten into a 0.9% growth year [4][25][26]. Leadership adds a second-order risk: Lagarde steps down after the February 2027 meeting, and a successor search during a supply shock raises the odds that the Council pauses at 2.75-3.00% [2]. Carry is therefore a persistent headwind for a euro holder - 137.5bp a year against the dollar and 200-210bp against NOK and AUD - and it is not set to fade before mid-2027. Strategically the factor stays Bearish at the same confidence: the differential is stable, and the risk around it is an ECB that stops early.

tactical.analysis: Euro-area HICP rose to 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August, with energy at 18.9%, services at 3.2% and core (excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) at 2.5% from 2.4%, so the overshoot is cost-push rather than demand-pull [2][8]. October country flashes were mixed: Italy's HICP jumped to 5.6%, France's to 3.8% and Spain held at 4.9%, but Germany fell to 2.8% as a fuel tax cut took effect, leaving consensus at 3.9% for the 4 November euro-area flash [7][8][26]. Q3 GDP surprised positively at +0.4% q/q against 0.2% expected and +1.3% y/y, with Q2 revised up to +0.6%, although France contracted 0.1% and Italy stagnated [9]. Germany grew 0.2% and Spain 0.6%, so the growth beat is concentrated in the periphery and Ireland (+5.5%) rather than in the two largest economies [9]. Forward indicators are softening: the October flash composite PMI fell to 51.9 from 53.1 against 52.7 expected, with services at 51.7, while the Ifo climate edged up to 90.2 on expectations (91.6) as current conditions slipped to 88.8 [11][12]. The labour market is loosening, with unemployment at 6.5% in September against 6.3% a year earlier and 122,000 more people out of work in the month [10]. Wages are not accelerating: compensation per employee slowed to 3.3% in Q2 from 3.6%, and the ECB wage tracker points to 2.5-2.8% for the rest of 2026 [2]. We expect the October flash at 3.9% headline and 2.5% core, in line with consensus, so the next data point is unlikely to move the ECB; the factor is Neutral because a hawkish inflation profile and a softening activity profile offset each other for the currency.

strategic.analysis: Over six months the inflation path is upward before it turns: UBS expects headline HICP to peak at 4.1% in January 2027, and the ECB's own survey of forecasters sees 3.0% for 2026 and 2.6% for 2027 with core at 2.4% and 2.5% [5][7]. That is a supply shock that erodes real incomes faster than nominal wages rise, since wages are tracking 2.5-2.8% against 3.8% inflation, a real wage squeeze of about 1 percentage point [2][8]. The ECB's 0.9% growth projection for 2026 already assumed high energy prices, but energy prices have risen further since the September cut-off and financing conditions have tightened by about 35bp at the 10-year point [2][4]. Bank lending growth slowed to 4.2% and mortgage lending to 3.0% in September, and credit standards tightened in Q3, so the transmission channel is biting [2]. France is the weak link: Q3 GDP fell 0.1%, its flash composite PMI was 48.4 in October and its fiscal plan requires EUR54bn of consolidation in 2027 [9][28]. Germany is the offset, with a 2027 budget that raises investment to EUR117.5bn and core defence spending to EUR109bn, a fiscal impulse that supports 2027 growth but arrives mainly after the strategic horizon [30]. The US comparison is unfavourable for the euro: US core PCE at 3.1% supports Fed hikes while US activity has not shown the euro area's energy drag, so the growth gap widens in the dollar's favour [34]. We expect euro-area growth of 0.1-0.2% q/q in Q4 and Q1 and headline inflation above 3.5% through March 2027, a stagflationary mix that is Bearish for the currency even as it keeps the ECB hawkish.

tactical.analysis: Risk appetite is deteriorating from a high base: the VIX rose from a 17.2 close to 20.05 in an intraday snapshot (about 12:18 ET) on 30 October, when the S&P 500 was 1.61% lower at 7,596.07 [7]. The VIX close of 17.2 on 29 October was 1.2 points above its level a month earlier and well inside a one-year range of 13.47 to 31.05, so volatility is elevated but not stressed. Credit is widening faster in Europe than in the US: the ICE BofA euro high-yield spread was 3.48% on 29 October against 2.94% a month earlier, after a one-year high of 3.64% on 23 October, while the US investment-grade spread was 0.89% [13][38]. The regime is transitioning from risk-on to risk-off, and the driver is specific: Washington has said strikes on Iran would not come before the 3 November midterms, and Brent was above $117 in the week to 27 October (best available, flagged: ICE front-month about $110.80 on 29 October; physical spot runs higher) [15]. The euro is not a haven; in October it fell 1.46% against the franc while the dollar strengthened, the pattern of a euro-specific stress episode rather than a dollar-smile move. Its risk beta in this regime is negative on two channels - higher energy prices and wider French spreads - and both were active in October, when the OAT-Bund spread reached a 15-year high [37]. The correlation structure is intact for the dollar but not for the euro's usual anti-dollar role, because the euro fell against every G10+SGD peer in October, not only the dollar. The three tail scenarios that would shift the regime are a post-midterm US strike on Iran (we estimate 35% within four weeks), a French government censure (20%) and a US-Iran deal that reopens Hormuz (15%); two of the three are euro-negative, so the factor is Bearish.

tactical.analysis: The terms-of-trade shock is the dominant euro-specific negative: Dutch TTF front-month gas traded at EUR100/MWh on 28 October for the first time since December 2022, about three times its pre-war level, and closed near EUR98 on 29 October; front-month settlements rose about 39% from about EUR72.4 on 30 September to EUR100.3 on 28 October (settlement levels best available, flagged, as of 2026-10-28) [14]. EU storage is only about 75% full and Germany's about 60% heading into winter, with LNG imports in the week to 9 October 30% below a year earlier, so the gas premium is supply-driven and persistent [14]. Brent was above $117 in the week to 27 October against about $72 before the war (best available, flagged; ICE front-month about $110.80 on 29 October), which adds an oil import bill on top of gas [15]. The trade balance has already turned: the euro area recorded a EUR16.1bn deficit in August, the largest since January 2023, as imports rose 16.7% y/y and petroleum imports 20.7% [17]. The current account surplus fell to EUR9bn in August from EUR27bn in July, and the 12-month sum to EUR250bn, or 1.5% of GDP (best available, flagged, as of August 2026), from 1.8% a year earlier [16]. Exports to the US remain strong at EUR39.3bn in August (+18.5% y/y) under the 15% US tariff ceiling agreed in 2025 and implemented in 2026, so trade policy is not the marginal driver [17][18]. German front-year power rose to EUR159.30/MWh and EU governments have spent EUR17.9bn on energy offsets this year, which shows the shock moving from trade into fiscal accounts [14]. For the next four weeks, with winter demand starting and storage below normal, the factor is Bearish with the joint-highest tactical confidence of the ten.

The 12-month surplus has already fallen from EUR290bn to EUR250bn (1.5% of GDP, best available, flagged, August 2026), and with August's monthly figure at EUR9bn the run-rate implies a further fall towards 1.0% of GDP by early 2027 [16]. The euro's largest export market, the US, took EUR39.3bn of goods in August, so a US slowdown would hit the one strong export channel [17]. Strategically the factor is Bearish at 60: a net energy importer facing a gas price near three times pre-war levels loses external support for its currency until either prices fall or demand adjusts.

tactical.analysis: The 29 October communication was a hawkish hold: the statement said energy prices 'have continued to rise' and pose upside risks to inflation, while committing to no particular rate path [1]. In the press conference Lagarde said the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate and decided unanimously to hold, and that if the current assessment holds 'the direction of travel is clear' [2]. Lagarde added that the decision 'does not indicate that we will not be hiking', which leans hawkish without any recorded dissent [7]. The ECB listed what it will see before December - new staff projections, two inflation prints, Q3 GDP, wage data, unemployment, industrial production, November PMIs and bank rate statistics - so guidance is explicitly data-dependent [2]. The market has bought the signal: December hike odds are above 80% and the euro briefly recovered from a 17-month low after Lagarde's comments [6]. The gap between guidance and pricing is therefore small for December; the ECB has not pushed back on about 75bp of total tightening priced, but it has not endorsed it either [5]. Credibility on inflation is intact - longer-term expectations remain around 2% even as short-horizon measures have risen [2]. Lagarde's announcement that she will step down after the February 2027 meeting adds a leadership question, but for the next four weeks the guidance and the pricing are aligned, so the factor is Neutral.

strategic.analysis: Over six months guidance credibility is the question of who sets it: Lagarde said 'My decision is to step down from my position as President of the European Central Bank' after the February 2027 meeting, and a successor search has begun [2]. Reuters reported she leaves on 7 February 2027, so the March 2027 meeting - where UBS expects the final hike to 3.00% - will be chaired by a new president or an interim arrangement [2][32]. Leadership transitions at the ECB have historically produced a cautious first meeting, which argues against a hike in March unless inflation is clearly above projections. The ECB's own projections imply limited need to go further: core HICP of 2.6% in 2027 and 2.3% in 2028, with headline at 2.1% in 2028 [4]. The Fed, by contrast, has two governors voting to hike and core PCE at 3.1%, so US guidance is more hawkish than the ECB's at the margin [33][34]. Markets price about 75bp of further ECB hikes against a UBS wealth-arm view that December is the last, a 50bp guidance-pricing gap if that view is right [5]. We expect the December projections to show 2027 headline inflation near 2.7% and core near 2.6%, which supports one hike but not a commitment to three. Strategically the factor is Bearish: market pricing is ahead of what the ECB's projections and its leadership calendar are likely to deliver.

tactical.analysis: The next four weeks contain three binary events with euro-negative skew. First, US midterms on 3 November: the White House said strikes on Iran would not come before them, and on 25 October Trump asked whether to 'make a deal' or 'finish them off' [15]. Second, the French budget: the Assembly votes on the revenue half on 3 November, unions strike on 5 November and the whole budget is due on 17 November, with a constitutional deadline on 17 December [28][29]. Prediction markets gave only a 44.5% chance of a French budget passing by 31 December on 31 October, and Article 49.3 would trigger an immediate censure motion that needs 289 votes [29]. Third, S&P reviews France on 27 November with the rating at A+ stable, after Moody's affirmed Aa3 negative on 23 October conditional on a deficit-reducing budget [28][37]. October already showed how these events transmit: the OAT-Bund spread reached a 15-year high and the euro hit a 17-month low in the same week [6][37]. We assign a 35% probability to a post-midterm US strike within four weeks (EUR/USD -1.0% to -1.5%), 20% to a censure of the Lecornu government (-0.8%) and 15% to a Hormuz reopening deal (+1.5%). Event volatility is not obviously priced: one-month implied at 6.33% exceeds 20-day realised by 1.6 vols, a modest premium for this calendar [40]. The probability-weighted outcome is negative, so the factor is Bearish.

Prediction markets on 31 October gave Le Pen a 41% (Polymarket) to 44% (Kalshi) chance of winning, and Macron's last term ends in May, so the French risk premium is likely to rise rather than fall through the strategic horizon [29]. Trade risk is lower than a year ago because the EU implemented the US deal with a 15% ceiling through 2029, though a safeguard clause allows suspension in defined circumstances [18]. German politics is stable relative to France, with a 2027 budget due for approval by year-end [30]. The net is Bearish: the dominant six-month event risks - a French political crisis and an energy escalation - are euro-negative, and the main positive, a durable Middle East settlement, has failed twice this year.

tactical.analysis: Fiscal risk is acute rather than background this month, centred on France. French public debt was EUR3,595.5bn or 119.0% of GDP at the end of Q2 2026, the 2026 deficit is expected at 5.4% of GDP, and the 2027 budget targets 5.0% with a EUR54bn effort [28][29]. The interest bill rises from EUR79.2bn in 2026 to EUR91.2bn in 2027, about EUR250m a day, and Agence France Tresor plans EUR340bn of medium- and long-term issuance in 2027 against EUR310bn in 2026 [28]. The French 10-year yield reached 5.14% on 23 October, the highest since July 2002, and the spread over Germany hit a 15-year high on 22-23 October, about 174bp at the peak on a daily benchmark-yield series (best available, flagged) [37]. Reuters put the premium at about 155bp on 29 October, still nearly double the 78bp of a year earlier [28][32]. Moody's affirmed Aa3 with a negative outlook on 23 October, assuming a deficit-reducing budget is adopted; Fitch and S&P rate France A+ stable [37]. Italy is the contrast: rated BBB+ with a positive outlook by S&P and Baa2 by Moody's, its spread was 109bp on 16 October against 80bp a year earlier [28][31], and about 114bp on 29 October on daily spread data (best available, flagged, 2026-10-29), so contagion is visible but contained. The ECB said its instruments, including the never-used Transmission Protection Instrument, are available against disorderly moves, but Lagarde stressed that high-debt countries must adapt to higher rates, which is not a signal of imminent support [1][2]. Tactically the factor is Bearish at 58, with sovereign CDS not available to us and the S&P review on 27 November the next rating catalyst.

strategic.analysis: Over six months the euro area's fiscal mix is deteriorating on two fronts. France's debt ratio is set to rise from 119.3% in 2026 to 121.7% in 2027 even if the budget passes, and higher issuance of EUR340bn meets a Eurosystem that no longer reinvests maturing bonds [1][29]. Germany is moving in the other direction on spending but not on credit quality: the 2027 draft budget borrows EUR203.6bn and plans EUR838.2bn of borrowing over 2027-2030, with interest costs rising from EUR41.9bn to EUR80.7bn by 2030 [30]. That expansion raises Bund supply and term premia, which helps explain why 10-year euro-area yields rose about 35bp after the September projections before October's haven rally [2]. Defence spending is rising to 2.8% of German GDP in 2026 and 3.5% by 2029, a structural fiscal stimulus that is growth-positive but adds supply across the bloc [30]. Italy's positive S&P outlook and a spread of 109-114bp leave it the more stable large periphery sovereign, the reverse of the 2011-12 pattern [31]. The rating calendar is skewed negatively: Moody's France outlook is negative and conditional on fiscal consolidation and lower financing costs, neither of which is assured before the 2027 election [37]. Strategically the factor is Bearish at 58 because French fiscal risk is now institutional, with an election in May 2027 that could reverse consolidation.

key_catalysts.priced_in: Mostly priced for the BoE; the strike is not

key_catalysts.rationale: With a December Fed hike at about 77% on a futures-derived calculation, a soft report would lower those odds and trigger euro short-covering; a strong one would push the pair through 1.1100.
key_catalysts.priced_in: Partially; the Fed path is the transmission

key_catalysts.rationale: US core PCE was 3.1% in September; a firm CPI print would raise December Fed odds above 85% and widen the expected policy gap.

key_catalysts.event: French National Assembly vote on the whole 2027 budget
key_catalysts.rationale: Prediction markets gave a budget by year-end only 44.5% on 31 October; a resort to Article 49.3 triggers an immediate censure motion needing 289 votes. A failed vote would push the OAT-Bund spread towards its 22-23 October 15-year high.
key_catalysts.priced_in: Partially: the spread near 155bp prices passage with difficulty

key_catalysts.event: ECB Account of the 28-29 October monetary policy meeting
key_catalysts.rationale: The Account will show how many members favoured a hike and whether the Council discussed the terminal rate; a hawkish tone could add about 5bp to December pricing.

key_catalysts.event: S&P Global review of France (A+ stable)
key_catalysts.rationale: Moody's affirmed Aa3 with a negative outlook on 23 October conditional on a deficit-reducing budget; S&P could move to a negative outlook if the budget stalls.
key_catalysts.priced_in: Not priced: the spread does not discount an outlook change

key_catalysts.rationale: Unemployment rose to 6.5% in September from 6.3% a year earlier; a rise to 6.6% would confirm labour-market loosening ahead of the ECB meeting.

key_catalysts.event: FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
key_catalysts.rationale: A hike to 4.00-4.25% with a dot plot showing another in 2027 would widen the policy gap to 150bp if the ECB moves only once.
key_catalysts.priced_in: About 77% on a futures-derived calculation of 30 October

key_catalysts.event: ECB Governing Council decision with staff projections
key_catalysts.rationale: We expect a 25bp hike to 2.75% (70%); the projections' 2027 inflation path decides whether markets keep about 75bp of total tightening priced. A hike framed as the last would be euro-negative despite the move.
key_catalysts.priced_in: December hike above 80% priced; the terminal is the swing

key_catalysts.event: French constitutional deadline for Parliament on the 2027 budget; BoE and Norges Bank decisions
key_catalysts.rationale: Missing the deadline leads to enactment by ordinance from 18 December or a stopgap special law, both of which undermine the 5.0% deficit target.
UBS expects headline inflation to peak at 4.1% in January 2027; a December print near 4% keeps a March hike alive.
We expect 0.1% q/q after 0.4% in Q3 as energy costs and tighter credit weigh on activity; a negative print would revive stagflation pricing.

key_catalysts.event: ECB Governing Council meeting, Lagarde's last as President
key_catalysts.rationale: Lagarde leaves on 7 February 2027; the successor's identity and first statements set the 2027 path, with a cautious first meeting the historical norm.

invalidators.condition: TTF front-month gas falls below EUR70/MWh and stays there for two weeks
invalidators.mechanism: the terms-of-trade shock that drives Factors 5 and 2 reverses, cutting the energy import bill and the inflation squeeze on real incomes.

invalidators.condition: the OAT-Bund 10-year spread falls below 120bp after a budget passes
invalidators.mechanism: the euro-specific fiscal and political premium that pushed the euro lower against every peer in October unwinds, removing the Factor 7 and 8 drag.

invalidators.condition: EUR/USD posts a weekly close above 1.1224
invalidators.mechanism: a close above the overhead resistance zone would show the speculative short being squeezed and would invalidate the break-of-1.1100 path.

invalidators.condition: the Fed holds on 9 December and signals a pause while the ECB hikes
invalidators.mechanism: the policy differential would narrow to 112.5bp and the relative path would turn euro-positive, removing the core of Factor 1.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: FOMC decision and US 2-year minus Schatz spread
invalidators.quantitative_threshold: Fed hold plus US 2Y-Schatz spread below 140bp

invalidators.condition: a US-Iran agreement reopens Hormuz and lifts the blockade for at least four weeks
invalidators.mechanism: Brent and TTF would fall sharply, the euro's energy discount would reverse and speculative shorts would cover from beyond their historical extreme.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Hormuz tanker transits and Brent front-month
invalidators.quantitative_threshold: Brent below $90 and TTF below EUR65/MWh

invalidators.condition: the 17 December ECB projections lift 2027 core HICP to 2.9% or above and the Council signals further hikes
invalidators.mechanism: a credible ECB path to 3.25% or higher would match market pricing (our sum of 2.50% and about 75bp priced) and remove the 25bp over-pricing behind Factors 1 and 6.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: ECB staff projections and the December statement

invalidators.condition: euro-area monthly current account returns above EUR30bn for two consecutive months
invalidators.mechanism: it would show the energy bill being absorbed without eroding the external surplus, removing the strategic Factor 5 driver.
invalidators.quantitative_threshold: Current account above EUR30bn in two consecutive months

factors_changed.reason: The composite PMI fell from a 41-month high of 53.1 to 51.9 and France contracted in Q3, offsetting the 0.4% GDP beat.
The October hold with 'the direction of travel is clear' aligned guidance with the more than 80% December pricing.
About 75bp of further ECB hikes is now priced against our 3.00% terminal, while the Fed's two hike dissents keep its path hawkish.
Headline HICP rose to 3.8% with wages at 2.5-2.8%, and credit conditions tightened in Q3.
The French budget lacks a majority, Le Pen's 2027 odds reached 41-44%, and the US has said Iran strikes are possible after the midterms.
Central-bank swap-line usage of $170m and reserves near $2.96tn show ample dollar liquidity; the Fed path is carried in Factor 1.

seasonality.pattern: The ECB's December staff projections are one of two annual rounds that most often reset the rate path (June is the other), and year-end brings seasonal dollar funding demand that typically lifts the cost of dollars for European banks from late November.
seasonality.historical_magnitude: We do not attach a reliable average return to either pattern; the December projection round matters through the size of the revision, and the year-end funding effect shows up in money-market spreads rather than a consistent EUR/USD move.
seasonality.current_alignment: Aligned with the bearish view: the December projections are more likely to frame a hike as late-cycle than to add hikes, and year-end dollar demand coincides with the Fed's 9 December decision.

assumptions: Spot levels, moving averages, realised volatilities, 52-week ranges and support and resistance zones are from weekday closing bars to 2026-10-30; realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days, and carry ratios are carry over 60-day realised volatility.

Implied volatility, risk reversals and butterflies are CME-listed euro FX option quotes observed on 2026-10-28; the implied-vol percentile is measured over the 49 observations available since 21 August 2026, not a full year. Forward points are derived from the CME futures roll (151.8bp annualised) on an actual/360 basis.

Bund yields are Trading Economics closes for 30 October (10-year 3.32%, 2-year 3.02%); a second daily benchmark series read 3.40% and 3.06% on the same day, an 8bp and 4bp source divergence, so the levels are best available, flagged.

The OAT-Bund spread is quoted at about 155bp on 29 October per Reuters and 137bp on 16 October per closing yields; the intramonth peak near 174bp on 22 October comes from a daily benchmark-yield series and is best available, flagged.

PPP fair values use World Bank PPP conversion factors (EUR 0.709983 per international dollar); they are long-run anchors and the factors could not be re-displayed at the source, so they are best available, flagged.

CFTC positioning is the Traders in Financial Futures report for the week to 27 October 2026 (released 30 October); percentiles are against the 26 weekly reports since 5 May 2026. The legacy non-commercial net is reported alongside because it is the measure with a long-run extreme of about -100,000 contracts.

Probabilities for central-bank decisions are our own estimates unless stated as market pricing (December ECB above 80% per Trading Economics; December Fed about 77% per a CME-method calculation of 30 October). Scenario probabilities, event probabilities and invalidator probabilities are our estimates.

No free source publishes 3M EUR/USD or JPY/USD cross-currency basis, euro-area sovereign CDS or Target2 balances on a current basis; these are documented gaps, and the futures roll is used as an upper bound on combined basis and expected-rate effects.

Peer macro figures are the latest published as of 2026-10-31: OECD releases for GDP, unemployment and current accounts, national statistics offices for CPI; euro-area October HICP had not been released as of the valuation date.
